v.q: How does the JVM decide an object can be garbage collected?
o: It is no longer reachable from any GC root
Its reference count has dropped to zero
It is older than a fixed number of seconds
Its `finalize()` method has been called
v.w: Java uses reachability tracing from roots (thread stacks, static fields, JNI). Cycles are collected fine because they are unreachable.

v.q: Which statement about reachability is NOT true?
o: An object is collected when its reference count is zero
Static fields are GC roots
Local variables on a thread stack are GC roots
A cycle of unreachable objects can be collected
v.w: The JVM does not count references. It traces from GC roots, which is why cycles are not a problem.

v.q: Why is the heap split into young and old generations?
o: Most objects die young, so frequent cheap young collections pay off
The operating system requires two separate memory regions
Strings must be kept apart from numbers in memory
Class definitions need their own generation
v.w: The weak generational hypothesis: collect the young generation often and cheaply, promote survivors to old, collect old rarely.

v.q: Which statement about generations is NOT true?
o: Most objects survive for a long time
Young collections are frequent and cheap
Surviving objects are promoted to the old generation
The weak generational hypothesis says most objects die young
v.w: The design relies on the opposite: most objects die young.

o: All application threads pause while the collector works
The JVM exits and restarts itself after a fatal error
A thread dump is written to disk for later analysis
A network call to another service times out
v.w: Modern collectors (G1, ZGC, Shenandoah) aim to keep pauses short by doing most of the work concurrently.

v.q: Which event is a stop-the-world pause?
o: All application threads stop during part of a collection
A request to another service times out
The JVM restarts after a crash
A thread waits for a database lock
v.w: During a pause the collector works while application threads are stopped. Shorter pauses are the goal of G1 and ZGC.

v.q: Which collector is the default in modern JDKs (9+) for server workloads?
o: G1
Serial
CMS
Epsilon
v.w: G1 splits the heap into regions and targets a pause-time goal. ZGC suits very large heaps with sub-millisecond pauses.

v.q: Which collector is designed for very short pauses on large heaps?
o: ZGC
Serial
Parallel
Epsilon
v.w: ZGC does most of its work concurrently and keeps pauses at about a millisecond regardless of heap size.

v.q: A service's heap usage keeps climbing and it ends with `OutOfMemoryError`, although it has no obvious bug. Which is the most likely cause?
o: A leak: objects stay reachable, e.g. in a static map or cache
The garbage collector has been switched off by a flag
The application has been given too few request threads
The disk has filled up with old log files and dumps
v.w: Java leaks are reachable objects that are no longer needed. Take a heap dump and look at the dominator tree.

v.q: Which observation points to a memory leak rather than too small a heap?
o: Old generation stays high after every full GC
Heap peaks and then drops to the same floor
Young collections run often
Pauses are short
v.w: A rising floor after full GC means objects remain reachable. A stable floor means the heap sizing is the issue.

v.q: Which tool or flag helps you capture evidence when an `OutOfMemoryError` occurs?
o: `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`, then inspect it in Eclipse MAT
`-Xmx0` to stop the heap from growing any further
Calling `System.gc()` repeatedly in a tight loop
Restarting the whole server once every single hour
v.w: The dump shows which objects dominate memory and what holds references to them.

v.q: Which option does NOT help you diagnose an OutOfMemoryError?
o: -Xmx0
A heap dump on OutOfMemoryError
GC logging
Eclipse MAT on a dump
v.w: A heap of zero cannot run an application. Dumps, logs and MAT show who holds the memory.

o: It only suggests a collection and may be ignored
It forces an immediate full collection every time
It frees native memory outside the heap
It resets the heap size to its default
v.w: Explicit GC calls can cause long pauses. Fix allocation patterns and tune the collector instead.

v.q: Which statement about System.gc() is NOT true?
o: It guarantees an immediate full collection
It is only a hint to the JVM
It may be ignored
It can be disabled with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC
v.w: The JVM may ignore it, so it gives no guarantee and is rarely a good idea.

v.q: A service has frequent long pauses caused by many large, short-lived allocations. What is a sensible first step?
o: Measure with GC logs, then cut allocation or tune settings
Sprinkle `System.gc()` calls through the code
Raise the number of request threads
Move the logs to a faster disk
v.w: Turn on GC logging (`-Xlog:gc*`), look at pause time and frequency, then change one thing at a time.

v.q: What should you do before tuning GC settings?
o: Collect GC logs and measure
Double the heap at random
Add System.gc() calls
Switch to ZGC first
v.w: Evidence shows whether the problem is allocation rate, heap size or a leak. Tuning without it is guesswork.
